# All definitions

## ND-01: Generation family `[EVOLVING]`

> A set of dev packages, one for each generation, whose payloads share one published name.

Issues: I-27.

A generation family is a set of dev packages, one for each generation, whose payloads all publish the same npm name. Each generation lives in its own directory below the directory of the family, named after the generation, as `host-contracts-cleartext/<vN>`. [D-02](../../../global/definitions/entries/D-02.md) defines a generation, and [ND-02](../entries/ND-02.md) says which generations of a family are live.

#### Examples

- ✅ `host-contracts-cleartext` is a generation family. `host-contracts-cleartext/<vN-1>` and `host-contracts-cleartext/<vN>` are two dev packages, and both payloads publish `@fhevm/host-contracts-cleartext`.
- ❌ `hardhat/v2/plugin` and `hardhat/v3/plugin` are not a generation family. Their directories follow the major versions of Hardhat, not the generations of the protocol, and their payloads publish two different names, `@fhevm/hardhat-plugin` and `@fhevm/hardhat-plugin-v3`.
- ❌ `common` is not a generation family. It is one shared helper, in one directory, with no generation in its path.

#### What can change

This definition follows the way the protocol rotates its generations. If the protocol design changes how generations are numbered or kept side by side, what makes a family can change too.

<a id="nd-02"></a>

## ND-02: Live generation `[EVOLVING]`

> A generation of a family that `npm-manifest.json#generations` names as `current` or `previous`.

Issues: I-27.

A live generation is a generation of a [generation family](../entries/ND-01.md) that `npm-manifest.json#generations` names for that family. The manifest names the directory of each one: `current` is `<vN>`, the generation that every consumer depends on, and `previous` is `<vN-1>`, kept so that the upgrade from `<vN-1>` to `<vN>` can be built and tested. A generation that the manifest no longer names is retired.

#### Examples

```jsonc
// ✅ Two live generations: current and previous.
"current": "./host-contracts-cleartext/<vN>",
"previous": "./host-contracts-cleartext/<vN-1>"
```

- ✅ After the rotation that brings in `<vN>`, `<vN>` and `<vN-1>` are the live generations of `host-contracts-cleartext`.
- ❌ `<vN-2>` is not live. The manifest no longer names it, so it is retired. A list that names the live generations, as the cleartext config of [NR-24](../../rules/entries/NR-24.md) does, never names `<vN-2>`.
- ❌ A directory that exists on disk is not live for that reason alone. Only the manifest makes a generation live.

#### Live on chain

In the npm workspace, a generation is live when the manifest names it, as above. Outside the workspace, "live" also means that a network runs it: a generation is live on chain on each network whose host contracts are at that generation. The two meanings follow different clocks:

- Liveness on chain is per network. A generation can be live on one network and dead on another.
- The workspace rotates when the developer starts the next generation, not when a network deploys one, as [NR-87](../../rules/entries/NR-87.md) says. So `current` can be live in the workspace before any network runs it.
- A generation that the workspace has retired can still be live on chain, on a network that has not upgraded yet.
- A generation that runs on no network any more is dead on chain for good.

Examples:

- ✅ Work on `<vN+1>` starts while testnet does not run `<vN>` yet. The workspace rotates anyway: `<vN+1>` is `current` and `<vN>` is `previous`, live in the workspace although no network runs either of them yet.
- ✅ After that rotation, mainnet can still run `<vN-1>`. `<vN-1>` is retired from the workspace and still live on chain on mainnet.
- ❌ Protocol v12 was retired from every network. It is dead on chain for good, and no workspace names it.

#### What can change

This definition follows the way the protocol rotates its generations. If the protocol design changes how many generations stay side by side, or how the manifest names them, which generations are live can change too.

## ND-03: Published package `[STABLE]`

> A package that leaves the workspace, through npm, a mirror repository, or both.

Aliases: published payload.

Issues: I-02, I-03, I-04, I-27.

A published package is a package that leaves the workspace. `npm-manifest.json` gives it the kind `published`, and its `distribution` names the channels through which it leaves: `npm`, `mirror`, or both. A published package with no `distribution` goes to npm only.

A published package does not always reach npmjs.com. A published package whose only channel is `mirror` is mirror-only: it reaches users through a public Git repository and never through npm. [ND-04](../entries/ND-04.md) defines the published packages that npm distributes.

#### Examples

```jsonc
// ✅ Published, through npm: no distribution means npm.
"./hardhat/v2/plugin/pkg": { "kind": "published", "name": "@fhevm/hardhat-plugin" }

// ✅ Published, mirror-only: it never reaches npmjs.com, and it is still published.
"./hardhat/v2/fhevm-hardhat-template/pkg": {
  "kind": "published",
  "name": "fhevm-hardhat-template-v2",
  "distribution": ["mirror"]
}

// ❌ Not published: a dev package stays in the workspace, even when it wraps a published package.
"./hardhat/v2/plugin": { "kind": "dev", "publishedRelPath": "./hardhat/v2/plugin/pkg" }
```

#### What can change

This definition follows the channels that the manifest schema allows in `distribution`. If the schema adds a channel, a published package can leave the workspace through it too.

<a id="nd-04"></a>

## ND-04: npm-distributed payload `[STABLE]`

> A published package that npm distributes, because its `distribution` names `npm` or is omitted.

Aliases: npm-distributed package.

Issues: I-03, I-27.

An npm-distributed payload is a [published package](../entries/ND-03.md) that reaches npmjs.com. Its `distribution` in `npm-manifest.json` includes `npm`, or is omitted, which means npm.

Being npm-distributed depends only on `distribution`. A published package can also be kept in sync with a Git repository through the `mirror` field of the manifest, and still be npm-distributed.

#### Examples

- ✅ `hardhat/v2/plugin/pkg`, published as `@fhevm/hardhat-plugin`. Its entry has no `distribution`, so npm distributes it.
- ✅ `foundry/forge-fhevm-std/pkg`, published as `@fhevm/forge`. Its entry has no `distribution`, so npm distributes it. It ships only Solidity sources, and is npm-distributed all the same.
- ✅ `host-contracts-cleartext/<vN>/pkg`, published as `@fhevm/host-contracts-cleartext`. Its entry has a `mirror` and no `distribution`, so npm distributes it, and the mirror does not change that.
- ❌ `hardhat/v2/fhevm-hardhat-template/pkg`. Its `distribution` is `["mirror"]`, so it is published but not npm-distributed.

#### What can change

This definition follows the `distribution` field of the manifest schema. If the schema changes how it names the npm channel, or the default when `distribution` is omitted, this definition changes with it.
